issues.legal_issue: An acquisition in which possession has been taken under the urgency power and the land has vested in the State does not lapse for failure to make an award within the period prescribed by Section 11-A, and the former owner cannot recover possession on that basis.
material_facts: The acquisition was made for a public scheme, and the inquiry was dispensed with under the urgency power.
Possession was taken and transferred for the scheme before an award was made.
The land vested in the State free from encumbrances.
The High Court held that the acquisition had lapsed because no award was made within two years and directed delivery of possession to the former owners.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to hold that the acquisition had lapsed or to direct delivery of possession. Section 11-A did not apply after possession had been taken under the urgency power and the land had vested in the State.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, taking possession under the urgency power results in the land vesting in the State free from encumbrances. Section 11-A does not cause an acquisition to lapse in such circumstances, and vesting is not undone by a later failure to make an award within the prescribed time. The Court relied on Lt. Governor of H.P. v. Avinash Sharma, Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., and Awadh Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquisition_lapse_order and urgent_acquisition_proceeding and possession_taken_before_award and land_vested_free_of_encumbrances

predicates.appeal_from_acquisition_lapse_order: A party appealed an order holding that an acquisition had lapsed and directing return of the land.
predicates.urgent_acquisition_proceeding: The acquiring authority used an urgency procedure to acquire the land.
predicates.possession_taken_before_award: The acquiring authority took possession before the award was made.
predicates.land_vested_free_of_encumbrances: After possession was taken, the land vested in the State free from encumbrances.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a lapse order and possession was taken in an urgency acquisition before the award, with the land having vested free from encumbrances, the acquisition does not lapse after vesting.

issues.legal_issue: Res judicata or estoppel does not prevent a court from giving effect to a statutory direction when a prior judgment would defeat that direction.
material_facts: A prior High Court order had declared the acquisition lapsed and directed delivery of possession.
The Supreme Court found that the acquisition had already vested in the State and that the prior direction was contrary to the applicable statutory rule.
The appeal challenged the legal effect of the High Court’s order.
issues.conclusion: The prior order did not bar the Court from giving effect to the statutory rule; res judicata and estoppel could not sustain the direction to return the land.
issues.legal_principle: A prior judgment cannot override or defeat a statutory direction or prohibition when giving effect to the judgment would conflict with that statutory command. The Court followed Municipal Committee, Amritsar v. State of Punjab, which it cited for the proposition that a prior decision does not operate as res judicata where the statutory defect or command governs the result.

rule.if: appeal_from_prior_order and prior_order_was_erroneous_on_its_face and statutory_command_applies and prior_order_would_defeat_statutory_command

predicates.appeal_from_prior_order: A party appealed an order that had already decided the dispute.
predicates.prior_order_was_erroneous_on_its_face: The reviewing court found that the earlier order was plainly inconsistent with the governing law.
predicates.statutory_command_applies: A statutory direction or prohibition governs the dispute.
predicates.prior_order_would_defeat_statutory_comma: Giving effect to the earlier order would prevent the statutory direction or prohibition from operating.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a plainly erroneous prior order and that order would defeat an applicable statutory command, the prior order does not bar the statutory result.

issues.legal_issue: Former owners whose land has been acquired are entitled to the interest specified by the Court but are not entitled to market value assessed as of the award date.
material_facts: The land was acquired and possession was taken before the award was made.
The Court addressed the former owners’ monetary entitlement while allowing the appeal with modifications.
issues.conclusion: The former owners were entitled to interest at 9% for one year from the date possession was taken and thereafter at 15% per annum until deposit into court, but were not entitled to market value as of the date of the award.
issues.legal_principle: The Court directed the stated interest entitlement and rejected a claim to market value as of the award date. The judgment does not identify a separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this specific compensation ruling; its discussion otherwise concerns the consequences of vesting under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.

predicates.land_acquired_and_possession_taken: The acquiring authority acquired the land and took possession of it.
predicates.compensation_entitlement_decided_in_acqu: An appeal concerning the acquisition also placed the former owners’ monetary entitlement before the court.

issues.definition: When an acquisition appeal decides the monetary entitlement of former owners whose land was acquired and possessed, they receive interest but not market value assessed as of the award date.
